To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) distributed roughness elements and scalloped edges are passive flow control strategies that reduce flow separation on the suction side of a NACA 643 airfoil at Re=64, 200, and α=8.6 deg; (2) distributed roughness results in high-frequency shedding that accelerates the transition of the separated flow, while the scalloped edge results in laminar separation bubbles that are situated in the troughs of the edge;
the large roughness elements result, in a first step, in an enhanced transition in the boundary layer.
the large roughness elements result, in the case of a 5% amplitude, in high-frequency shedding that results in an accelerated boundary layer transition.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of passive flow control methods for airfoil applications.
the numerical investigation of passive flow control strategies for an airfoil at low-Reynolds-number conditions.
the numerical simulation of passive flow control strategies for a modified NACAA643-618 airfoild at a chord-based Reynold number of Re= 64,200 and a 0= 8.64 deg.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the flow physics are different for the two different control strategies.
the flow physics and performance enhancement of passive separation control for the airfoil at the considered conditions are very different.
the scalloped airfoil with 5% amplitude of the leading-edge serration has the best performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we investigated the effect of passive separation control strategies on the aerodynamic performance and flow physics of a NACA 643–618 airfoil at low Reynolds numbers.
passive flow control strategies can be successfully used for airfoils at low-Reynolds-number conditions.
the scalloped airfoils are more effective than distributed roughness elements.
The main takeaway from our work is that
passive control strategies can be used to enhance the aerodynamic performance of airfoils at low-Reynolds-number conditions.
the flow physics of the two passive flow control methods are different, and that they result in different performance enhancements.
the scalloped airfoil with 5% amplitude of the serration results in a drag reduction of 20% and a lift increase of 20%, while Rek=446 only results in a 10% drag reduction and a lift increase.
